paras: The killing of Fred Ludeling was the fatal shooting of Fred L. Ludeling, son of former Louisiana chief justice John T. Ludeling, and the wounding of his cousin Frank Dinkgrave on the neighboring Stubbs place on Bayou DeSiard, near Monroe in Ouachita Parish, on March 17, 1881. It followed a dispute over moving a Black family from the Stubbs place to the Ludeling place, and the four men tried for the murder were acquitted. Northern Republican papers called it a political assassination, while the Monroe press treated it as a personal quarrel between two planters.

Judge Ludeling and F. P. Stubbs owned adjoining places, and in early March their lawsuit ended in a courtroom brawl with thrown chairs. A Washington dispatch in the New-York Tribune said Stubbs's hands had wanted to leave for Ludeling's place for better treatment, and that Stubbs kept men to stop them. W. B. Mitchner, who managed the Stubbs place, had sent word not to interfere with his labor.

On the morning of March 17 two wagons went from the Ludeling place to move a woman and a boy, sent, Dinkgrave testified, by him. The woman, Susan Davis, testified that she had agreed to go to the house of Wallace, a Black man on the Ludeling place. The wagons were cut down, "presumably by Mr. Mitchner," and Dinkgrave and Ludeling rode over to recover them.

In Dinkgrave's sworn account, five men were at the cabin, Mitchner cursed the riders, and after an exchange of insults with Ludeling he drew his pistol and fired the first shot at him. Dinkgrave fired once, was shot through both arms, and was chased up the road by Kirkpatrick until Black men carried him into Shultz's store. Ludeling died with five wounds in the neck and one in the arm, and Mitchner was shot through the side.

A coroner's jury found that Ludeling died of a gunshot wound. On Dinkgrave's affidavit, six men including Mitchner, George Mitchner, Linton Stubbs, A. S. Brown and S. S. Kirkpatrick were charged with murder but not held in custody. At the hearing Susan Davis swore that Mitchner fired first, and R. M. Scott said he had seen four of the accused riding with shotguns shortly before the shooting. The grand jury later ignored the bill against Kirkpatrick.

Four men went to trial on April 21 before a jury that included two Black men. The defense argued self-defense and "premeditated aggression" by Ludeling and Dinkgrave, and on April 28 the jury acquitted them to slight applause. Judge Ludeling then charged in a public letter that "a system of peonage and terrorism" existed in the parish, and Stubbs replied that the killing was personal.

New Orleans wires reported a "serious difficulty," and the Washington Evening Star headed one dispatch "Murdered by the Overseer." Within a week the Portland Daily Press blamed "Southern political assassins," the Mankato Free Press ran "Killed by Bulldozers," and the Princeton Union called it "Another Political Murder." A Minnesota crime column said the young men were shot protecting "negro laborers" from "a mob of roughs."

The Ouachita Telegraph wrote that the laborers were willing to leave, "as negroes too often will do," and called the political interpretation "too absurd for notice or denial." During the trial it praised the accused for their "dignity and composure." The Donaldsonville Chief first reprinted the Telegraph's account but in June, under "Bulldozed Ouachita," found Judge Ludeling's charges credible.
After the acquittal the Daily Kennebec Journal and the Vermont Phoenix printed Mrs. Ludeling's account, in which her son was called "a nigger-loving Radical" before he was shot.

Dinkgrave and Susan Davis swore that Mitchner fired first, but the Claiborne Guardian, writing before the hearing, said Black onlookers declared Mitchner did not shoot and no one knew who began. The defense held that Ludeling and Dinkgrave were the aggressors. Mrs. Ludeling's version said David Wallace had borrowed the wagons to fetch his intended wife and fled after the overseer's threats.

reader.title: Killing of Fred Ludeling
bases: The shooting arose when wagons from the Ludeling place came to remove a Black family of laborers from the Stubbs place and the Stubbs manager cut them down (A10, A12); those shot were the Ludeling party, not the laborers.

Wire reports, the Monroe paper, a Homer editor's inquiries and sworn hearing testimony agree that Ludeling was killed and Dinkgrave wounded on the Stubbs place on March 17 (A5, A7, A10, A12), though who fired first and why are disputed (A7, A20).

accounts.label: Susan Davis (Black witness)
accounts.gist: From the cabin gallery she saw W. B. Mitchner fire the first shot and then saw Ludeling fall.

accounts.label: Homer editor's inquiries at Monroe
accounts.gist: Black onlookers said Mitchiner did not shoot; Dinkgrave was said to have shot Mitchiner; no one knew who killed Ludeling or fired first, and he seemed shot from the rear.

accounts.label: Monroe paper
accounts.gist: Hot and angry words followed the cutting of the wagons and led to shooting, in a quarrel between two planters.

accounts.label: Defense
accounts.gist: The accused acted in self-defense against premeditated aggression by Ludeling and Dinkgrave.

accounts.label: Mrs. Ludeling's letter
accounts.gist: David Wallace borrowed the wagons to fetch his intended wife; the overseer's threats drove the Black men off; Ludeling, called 'a nigger-loving Radical', was riddled with buckshot.

accounts.label: Northern Republican telegram
accounts.gist: A political assassination by desperadoes Stubbs employed to keep his laborers from leaving for Ludeling's place.
